_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 154 - Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), chs. 8-11: Dissensions at Hawaiki (123-131), Poutini and Whaiapu / Discovery of New Zealand (132-134), Construction of Canoes (134-135), The Voyage to New Zealand (136-151). Topics 4 founding legends, 8 trickster. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Whakaturia Dances His Way Out of the Smoke

region.zh: 哈瓦基烏努庫之村（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 8, The Quarrels at Hawaiki (London 1855)

summary.en: The dog of Houmai-tawhiti eats the sloughed matter of Uenuku's ulcer and is killed, howling its death inside Toi-te-huatahi's belly - the origin of the proverb 'hush, hush, I thought I had hid you in the big belly of Toi'. In revenge Tama-te-kapua and Whakaturia steal Uenuku's poporo fruit nightly on stilts. Caught, Whakaturia is hung in the smoke of the meeting-house; coached through a hole in the thatch, he wins a stage to dance, secures Uenuku's red apron and carved sword, and leaps from the house while Tama bolts the door behind them. The cycle of feud that ends in the migration begins here.
summary.zh: 豪邁陶維提之犬吞食烏努庫潰瘍剝落之物，被殺後在圖伊特胡阿塔希腹中哀嚎——『噓、噓！我本以為把你藏進圖伊的大肚子，你這可恨的東西還在嚎』一諺由此而生。塔馬特卡普亞兄弟以高蹺夜偷烏努庫的波波羅果被擒；瓦卡圖里亞被吊在大屋炊煙之上。兄長從屋頂鑿孔傳授計策：先討油梳髮插羽，再討紅裙寶劍；舞蹈至門邊，一躍而出——塔馬自外閂門，兄弟雙雙逃脫，哈瓦基世代血仇由此而起。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; foundational feud legend of the Arawa migration cycle.

passages.text: In the time of Houmai-tawhiti there had been a great war, and many battles were fought in Hawaiki; the troubles had arisen from the act of desecration committed by the dog of Houmai-tawhiti and of his sons in eating the matter that had sloughed from an ulcer of Uenuku's. When Toi-te-huatahi and Uenuku saw the dog, named Potaka-tawhiti, do this, they killed it; and the sons of Houmai-tawhiti, missing the dog, went searching from village to village. At last the dog howled in the belly of Toi', 'Ow!' - again and again, however tight the old man held his mouth shut - and Toi' said, and his words passed into a proverb: 'Oh, hush, hush! I thought I had hid you in the big belly of Toi', and there you are, you cursed thing, still howling away.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 8 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as the two brothers got home they began immediately to make stilts for Tama-te-kapua, and started that night for the village of Toi' and Uenuku, arriving at Uenuku's fine poporo tree; they remained eating its fruit a good long time, and continued this every night, until Uenuku and his people found the fruit nearly all gone, and traces of Tama's stilts. They kept watch; and whilst one party came to steal, the other lay in wait, and caught both of them - Whakaturia at the very foot of the tree, and Tama' on the sea-shore after a chase. Those holding Tama' cried that some should chop down his stilts with an axe so the fellow might fall into the water; but Tama' called down, 'If you fell me in the water I shall not be hurt, but if you cut me down on shore the fall will kill me' - so they cut him down on shore, and in a moment he was on his feet and off like a bird escaped from a snare.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 8 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The village assembled to see Whakaturia put to death; instead of killing him at once they hung him up in the roof of Uenuku's house to be stifled by the smoke, kindling a fire and dancing and singing shockingly bad every night. A report reached his brother, who climbed by night upon the roof, made a little hole in the thatch over the spot where his brother hung, and whispered with him. He coached him: complain of their dancing, claim to dance better; ask for oil to dress the hair, feathers for the head, the red apron of Uenuku and his carved two-handed sword; then dance. When they were all given, Whakaturia stood up and danced, looking bright and beautiful as the morning star, his eyes flashing like the mother-of-pearl eyes in the sword's carved handle. At the door he said quietly he was dying with heat and the door should be slid back; then, as is the custom in the dance, he turned right and left making hideous faces, sprang about, and made a spring from the inside of the house - immediately he was beyond the door. Up sprang Tama-te-kapua and instantly bolted it; Whakaturia helped him bolt the window, and there they heard those inside cursing like a hole full of young parrots, whilst away ran Tama' and his brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 8 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Ngahue and the Fish of Greenstone

region.en: Arahura River, West Coast, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭西岸阿拉胡拉河（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 9, The Legend of Poutini and Whaiapu / The Discovery of New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Hine-tu-a-hoanga, whose stone is obsidian, drives out Ngahue and his greenstone Poutini; pursuing him island to island, she forces him to seek a place where his jasper may rest in peace - and he finds the island Aotearoa, making Arahura an everlasting resting-place for greenstone. Breaking off a portion, he returns to Hawaiki reporting a new country that produces the moa and jasper in abundance, and from his block - the 'fish of Ngahue' - the axes Tutauru and Hauhau-te-rangi are ground, with which the migration canoes are hewn.
summary.zh: 黑曜石之主希內圖阿洪阿驅逐碧玉主人恩加胡埃，一路追趕；恩加胡埃為其碧玉尋找安息之地，終在海上發現奧特亞羅亞島（紐西蘭北島），並以西岸阿拉胡拉為碧玉永恆之家。他掰下一塊帶回哈瓦基，報告新大陸盛產恐鳥與碧玉；後人以其石塊——『恩加胡埃之魚』——磨成圖陶魯與豪豪特朗吉雙斧，正是用它們砍鑿了移民大舟。

sensitivity.note: Poutini (greenstone) and Whaiapu (obsidian) are stone beings; the record explains both pounamu sources and the discovery chain of the migration.

passages.text: For a long time Poutini and Whaiapu both rested in the same place, and Hine-tu-a-hoanga, to whom the stone Whaiapu belonged, became excessively enraged with Ngahue and with his stone Poutini. At last she drove Ngahue out and forced him to leave the place, and he departed to a strange land taking his jasper. When she saw he was departing with his precious stone she followed after them; Ngahue arrived at Tuhua with his stone, and Hine-tu-a-hoanga landed there at the same time with him and began to drive him away again. Then Ngahue went to seek a place where his jasper stones might remain in peace, and he found in the sea this island Aotearoa, the northern island of New Zealand, and thought he would land there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 9 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: He thought again, lest he and his enemy should be too close to one another and quarrel again, that it would be better for him to go further off with his jasper, a very long way off. So he carried it off with him, they coasted along, and at length arrived at Arahura on the west coast of the middle island, and he made that an everlasting resting-place for his jasper. Then he broke off a portion of his jasper and took it with him, returning by Wairere, Whangaparaoa and Tauranga, direct to Hawaiki, and reported that he had discovered a new country which produced the moa and jasper in abundance. He manufactured sharp axes from his jasper - two axes, Tutauru and Hauhau-te-rangi - and fashioned portions into neck and ear ornaments; the ear ornament Kaukau-matua was lost only in 1846 when Te Heuheu was killed with so many of his tribe by a landslip.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 9 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Ngahue, returning, arrived again in Hawaiki, he found them all engaged in war; when they heard his description of the beauty of this country of Aotea, some of them determined to come here. All these axes were made from the block of green stone brought back by Ngahue to Hawaiki, which was called 'The fish of Ngahue'; he had previously come to these islands from Hawaiki when he was driven out from thence by Hine-tu-a-hoanga, whose fish or stone was obsidian, with which the natives grind down the jasper. The canoes which afterwards arrived here came in consequence of his discovery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 9 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: The Canoes of the Great Migration Are Hewn

region.zh: 哈瓦基之拉羅湯加（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 10, Construction of Canoes to Emigrate to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: In Rarotonga a totara is felled and the Arawa hewn by Rata, Wahie-roa, Ngahue and Paiata; Hotu-roa borrows the workmen and gains the Tainui. The fleet is named - Arawa, Tainui, Matatua, Taki-tumu, Kura-hau-po, Toko-maru, Matawhaorua - the canoes in which the forefathers crossed the ocean to Aotea-roa, all cut with Ngahue's greenstone axes, one of which, Tutauru, was the axe that cut off the head of Uenuku. But Rata slew the son of Manaia and hid his body in the chips and shavings of the canoes, planting a new curse in the exodus.
summary.zh: 眾人在拉羅湯加伐倒一棵羅漢松，由拉塔、瓦希耶羅亞、恩加胡埃、派亞塔等人鑿成阿拉瓦號；霍圖羅亞借得工匠，遂得泰努伊號。七艘大舟——阿拉瓦、泰努伊、馬塔圖亞、塔基圖穆、庫拉豪波、托科馬魯、馬塔瓦奧魯阿——載著先祖橫渡重洋。斧皆出自恩加胡埃碧玉，其中圖陶魯正是砍下烏努庫頭顱之斧。然拉塔殺死馬納亞之子、屍藏木屑之中，大遷徙中又埋下新的詛咒。

sensitivity.note: Founding-legend record for the Arawa/Tainui canoe traditions.

passages.text: They then felled a totara tree in Rarotonga, which lies on the other side of Hawaiki, that they might build the Arawa from it. The tree was felled, and thus the canoe was hewn out from it and finished. The names of the men who built this canoe were Rata, Wahie-roa, Ngahue, Paiata, and some other skilful men, who helped to hew out the Arawa and to finish it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 10 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: A chief of the name of Hotu-roa, hearing that the Arawa was built and wishing to accompany them, came to Tama-te-kapua and asked him to lend him his workmen to hew out some canoes for him too, and they went and built and finished the Tainui and some other canoes. These are the workmen who built the canoes in which the forefathers crossed the ocean to this island, to Aotea-roa. The names of the canoes were as follows: the Arawa was first completed, then Tainui, then Matatua, and Taki-tumu, and Kura-hau-po, and Toko-maru, and Matawhaorua. These are the names of the canoes in which the forefathers departed from Hawaiki and crossed to this island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 10 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they had lashed the topsides on to the Tainui, Rata slew the son of Manaia and hid his body in the chips and shavings of the canoes. The names of the axes with which they hewed out these canoes were Hauhau-te-Rangi and Tutauru; Tutauru was the axe with which they cut off the head of Uenuku. All these axes were made from the block of green stone brought back by Ngahue to Hawaiki, which was called 'The fish of Ngahue'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 10 (1855); not verbatim.

title.zh: 塔馬特卡普亞拐走祭司

region.zh: 哈瓦基啟航海灘（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Realizing the Arawa has no priest, Tama-te-kapua asks Ngatoro-i-rangi aboard 'to perform the necessary religious rites', lures his wife Kearoa too, and orders anchor raised the moment both are on deck. He tricks Ruaeo likewise: fetch my axe Tutauru from under the window-sill - and sails away with Ruaeo's wife as well. Two thefts, and the proverb: a descendant of Tama-te-kapua will steal anything he can.
summary.zh: 阿拉瓦號起航在即，塔馬特卡普亞發現船上無祭司，便以『行必要宗教儀式』為名，誘泰努伊號首領恩加托羅伊蘭基登舟，又以潔舟獻祭為由喚其妻基亞羅亞同來——二人才踏上甲板，他便喝令起錨張帆。他同樣戲耍魯亞奧：『替我取窗檻下的斧子吧』——待魯亞奧返回，舟已遠去，其妻也被擄走。兩樁偷竊，一諺流傳：塔馬特卡普亞的子孫，見物就偷。

passages.text: When the canoes were built and ready for sea, they were dragged afloat, the separate lading of each canoe was collected and put on board, with all the crews. Tama-te-kapua then remembered that he had no skilful priest on board his canoe, and thought the best thing he could do was to outwit Ngatoro-i-rangi, the chief who had command of the Tainui. So just as his canoe shoved off, he called out to Ngatoro, 'I say, Ngatoro, just come on board my canoe, and perform the necessary religious rites for me.' Then the priest Ngatoro came on board, and Tama-te-kapua said he had better also call his wife Kearoa, that she might make the canoe clean or common with an offering of seaweed laid in the canoe instead of an offering of fish, for the second fish caught in a canoe, or seaweed, or some substitute, ought to be offered for the females, the first for the males.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ngatoro assented to all this and called his wife, and they both got into Tama's canoe. The very moment they were on board, Tama' called out to the men, 'Heave up the anchors and make sail', and he carried off with him Ngatoro and his wife, that he might have a priest and wise man on board his canoe. Then they up with the fore-sail, the main-sail, and the mizen, and away shot the canoe. Up came Ngatoro and said, 'Shorten sail, that we may go more slowly, lest I miss my own canoe'; but Tama' replied, 'Oh no, wait a little, and your canoe will follow after us'; for a short time it kept near them, but soon dropped more and more astern, and each canoe proceeded on its own course.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Two thefts were perpetrated by Tama-te-kapua: he carried off the wife of Ruaeo, and Ngatoro and his wife, on board the Arawa. He made a fool of Ruaeo too, saying, 'Oh, Rua', you, like a good fellow, just run back to the village and fetch me my axe Tutauru; I pushed it in under the sill of the window of my house.' Rua' was foolish enough to run back; then off went Tama' with the canoe, and when Rua' came back again, the canoe was so far off that its sails did not look much bigger than little flies. So he fell to weeping for all his goods on board the canoe, and for his wife Whakaoti-rangi, whom Tama-te-kapua had carried off as a wife for himself. Hence this proverb: 'A descendant of Tama-te-kapua will steal anything he can.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

region.zh: 阿拉瓦號航程大漩渦（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Insulted that Tama-te-kapua laid hands on his wife, the priest Ngatoro climbs the roof of the deckhouse and changes the stars of evening into the stars of morning, raising winds to drive the Arawa backwards until it dashes into the whirlpool called the Throat of Te Parata - 'the steep descent where the world ends'. Only when the crew's shrieks move him does he lift the canoe out by incantation; most of the lading is lost, whence the proverb of the half-filled basket of Whakaoti-rangi.
summary.zh: 祭司恩加托羅因妻受辱，登上艙房屋頂，將暮星化作晨星，呼起逆風逼使阿拉瓦號倒退，直衝入名為『特帕拉塔之喉』的大漩渦——即『世界盡頭之陡淵』。船頭沒頂，貨物滾落入海；他聽聞婦孺哭號、船員哀呼，方才動了惻隱之心，誦咒平息風浪，將獨木舟從漩渦中拔出。輜重盡失，僅存半籃口糧——『瓦卡奧蒂蘭基的半籃』一諺由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Deluge-adjacent peril episode within the migration cycle; the priest's star inversion is recorded as a magical feat.

passages.text: Before climbing upon the roof Ngatoro suspected treachery about his wife, for he had found out what a treacherous person Tama-te-kapua was; so he took a string and tied one end of it to his wife's hair and kept the other in his hand, then climbed to the top of the roof. He had hardly got there when Tama' laid hold of his wife, and cunningly untied the end of the string and made it fast to one of the beams of the canoe; Ngatoro, feeling it tight, thought his wife had not moved. Coming down, he found the string tied fast to the beam, and asked his wife, 'Has not some one disturbed you?' She answered, 'Cannot you tell that from the string being fastened to the beam of the canoe? Who was it, indeed? Could it be any one else but Tama-te-kapua?' Her husband said, 'You are a noble woman indeed thus to confess this; since he has dealt in this way, I will now have my revenge on him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then that priest went forth upon the roof of the house and stood there, and called aloud to the heavens in the same way that Rua' did, and he changed the stars of the evening into those of morning, and he raised the winds that they should blow upon the prow of the canoe and drive it astern, and the crew were at their wits' end and quite forgot their skill as seamen, and the canoe drew straight into the whirlpool called 'The throat of Te Parata' - which the people of New Zealand also call 'the steep descent where the world ends' - and dashed right into that whirlpool. The canoe became engulfed; the waters reached the first bailing place in the bows, then the second bailing place in the centre, and the canoe appeared to be going down head foremost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Up sprang Tama-te-kapua in despair, shouting, 'Oh, Ngatoro, the canoe is gone down so much by the bow that Kearoa's pillow has rolled from under her head.' The priest heard them, but neither moved nor answered until he heard the goods rolling from the decks and splashing into the water, the crew holding on with great difficulty, some having already fallen into the sea. When these things took place, the heart of Ngatoro was moved with pity, for he heard the shrieks of the men and the weeping of the women and children. Then up stood that mighty man again, and by his incantations changed the aspect of the heavens so that the storm ceased, and he repeated another incantation to draw the canoe back out of the whirlpool. Lo, the canoe rose up floating rightly; but a great part of its lading had been thrown out into the water, and a great part of their provisions lost. Thence comes the native proverb when they can give a stranger but little food: 'Oh, it is the half-filled basket of Whakaoti-rangi, for she only managed to save a very small part of her provisions.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

title.zh: 旺加帕羅亞擱淺鯨之爭

region.zh: 紐西蘭東角旺加帕羅亞

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Landing at Whangaparaoa, the weary crews see pohutukawa trees in full red flower and take them for head-ornaments; Tauninihi throws his real red plumes into the sea, and the flowers crumble at a touch - the origin of the proverb of the red head-ornament found by Mahina. The crews then find a fresh stranded sperm whale and dispute the claim; the test of the thanksgiving altars - Tainui's posts dried over fire, Arawa's posts green - awards the whale to Tainui, who had already tied a rope to its jaw.
summary.zh: 兩舟先後抵達旺加帕羅亞：船員誤將盛開的紅花新西蘭聖誕樹當作頭飾，陶尼尼希遂將真紅羽飾拋入海中——上岸方知所謂紅飾不過落花，『馬希那撿到的紅頭飾，有借無還』一諺由此而來。海灘上橫著一頭新擱淺的抹香鯨，兩族人爭執誰先登陸誰先發現；遂以各自感恩祭壇之木檢驗——泰努伊的柱子經火烤乾，阿拉瓦的柱子猶帶青色——鯨歸泰努伊，其繩索早已拴上鯨顎。

sensitivity.note: First-landing dispute ritualized through altar-post inspection.

passages.text: Then they sailed on and landed at Whanga-Paraoa, in Aotea here. As they drew near to land they saw with surprise some pohutukawa trees of the sea-coast covered with beautiful red flowers, and the still water reflected back the redness of the trees. One of the chiefs of the canoe cried out to his messmates, 'See there, red ornaments for the head are much more plentiful in this country than in Hawaiki, so I'll throw my red head ornaments into the water'; and so saying he threw them into the sea. The name of that man was Tauninihi, and the name of the ornament was Taiwhakaea. The moment they got on shore they ran to gather the pohutukawa flowers, but no sooner did they touch them than the flowers fell to pieces; then they found out that these red head ornaments were nothing but flowers. Shortly afterwards the ornaments of Tauninihi were found by Mahina on the beach of Mahiti, who would not give them up - thence the proverb for anything lost and found by another: 'I will not give it up, 'tis the red head ornament which Mahina found.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as the party landed at Whanga-Paraoa they planted sweet potatoes, that they might grow there; and they are still to be found growing on the cliffs at that place. Then the crew, wearied from the voyage, wandered idly along the shore, and found the fresh carcase of a sperm whale stranded upon the beach. The Tainui had already arrived in the same neighbourhood; when they met they began to dispute as to who had landed first and first found the dead whale, and as to which canoe it consequently belonged to.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: To settle the question they agreed to examine the sacred place which each party had set up to return thanks to the gods for their safe arrival, that they might see which had been longest built; and doing so, they found that the posts of the sacred place put up by the Arawa were quite green, whilst the posts of the sacred place set up by the Tainui had evidently been carefully dried over the fire before they were fixed in the ground. The people who had come in the Tainui also showed part of a rope which they had made fast to its jaw-bone. When these things were seen, it was admitted that the whale belonged to the people who came in the Tainui, and it was surrendered to them. Whanga-Paraoa means the bay of the sperm whale, so called from the whale found there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Marama Pins the Tainui at the Portage
title.zh: 瑪拉瑪咒釘泰努伊於搬運道

region.zh: 奧塔胡胡搬運道，塔馬基地峽（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Surprised by sea-birds flying westward, the Tainui crews explore and find a vast sheet of salt water behind them, and resolve to drag their canoes over the Otahuhu portage. Toko-maru crosses easily; but Hoturoa's wife Marama-kiko-hura, unwilling that the tired crews should go further, fixes the Tainui to the earth by enchantment so that no human strength can stir it. At last Hoturoa's other wife, more learned in magic, chants a far more powerful incantation, and the canoe glides over the skids to float on the Manukau and settle at Kawhia.
summary.zh: 泰努伊眾人在塔馬基河口見海鷗蠣鷸自西飛來，探索之下發現身後竟有一大片鹹水，遂決定拖舟越過奧塔胡胡搬運道。托科馬魯號輕鬆過關；泰努伊號卻紋絲不動——霍圖羅亞之妻瑪拉瑪基科胡拉不願疲憊的船員再遠行，以咒術將其釘死於地，人力盡施亦不能撼動。直至霍圖羅亞另一位更精於法術之妻誦出更強咒語，大舟方滑過墊木，駛入馬努考港，最後安家卡菲亞。

sensitivity.note: Explains the Tainui waka's landfall at Kawhia and the naming of the portage.

passages.text: The Tainui left Whanga-Paraoa shortly after the Arawa, made the Gulf of Hauraki, coasted to Cape Brett, to the island with an arched passage through it called Motukokako, and on to Muriwhenua near the North Cape. Finding the land ended there, they returned along the coast until they reached the Tamaki, landed there, and proceeded up the creek to Tau-oma, the portage, where they were surprised to see flocks of sea-gulls and oyster-catchers passing over from the westward. They went off to explore in that direction and found, to their great surprise, a large sheet of water lying immediately behind them; so they determined to drag their canoes over the portage at a place they named Otahuhu and launch them again on the vast sheet of salt-water they had found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first canoe which they hauled across was the Toko-maru - that they got across without difficulty. They next began to drag the Tainui over the isthmus; they hauled away at it in vain, they could not stir it; for one of the wives of Hoturoa, named Marama-kiko-hura, who was unwilling that the tired crews should proceed further on this new expedition, had by her enchantments fixed it so firmly to the earth that no human strength could stir it. They hauled, they hauled, they excited themselves with cries and cheers, but they hauled in vain, they cried aloud in vain, they could not move it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When their strength was quite exhausted by these efforts, another of the wives of Hoturoa, more learned in magic and incantations than Marama-kiko-hura, grieved at seeing the exhaustion and distress of her people, rose up and chanted forth an incantation far more powerful; then at once the canoe glided easily over the carefully-laid skids, and it soon floated securely upon the harbour of Manuka. The willing crews urged on the canoes with their paddles, soon discovered the mouth of the harbour on the west coast, passed out into the open sea, coasted southwards, and discovering the small port of Kawhia, entered it and, hauling up their canoe, fixed themselves there for the time, whilst the Arawa was left at Maketu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

region.en: Maketu beach, Bay of Plenty, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭豐盛灣馬凱圖海灘

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Ruaeo, following in his own canoe, reaches Maketu first, hooks the sleeping Arawa ashore with a fishing line, and plays his flute beneath her side until his stolen wife wakes and confesses. He coaches her to complain of a dream of his flute-playing, so that the jealous Tama-te-kapua strikes her; she flies to Ruaeo. At dawn his incantations keep the whole crew asleep; at noon he raps the hull, and 140 feather-clad warriors appear beneath the canoe. He challenges Tama-te-kapua to single combat, dashes him four times to the earth, and rubs a prepared heap of vermin into the giant's hair - 'keep the woman', he says, 'as payment for the insults I have heaped upon you' - and departs with his men.
summary.zh: 魯亞奧駕自己的普凱阿特瓦伊努伊號後發先至馬凱圖，用釣鉤將沉睡的阿拉瓦號拖上岸，在船舷下吹笛，喚醒被擄之妻並授以計策。清晨他以咒術令全船沉睡；正午以棒擊船，一百四十名羽飾勇士赫然現於船下。他向塔馬特卡普亞單獨挑戰，四次將其摔倒，最後把備好的寄生蟲抹進這位九尺巨人的頭髮：『女人留給你，算作我羞辱你的賠禮。』言畢率眾而去。

sensitivity.note: Grey notes the giants: Tama-te-kapua nine feet, Ruaeo eleven feet tall.

passages.text: Ruaeo, who had already arrived at Maketu, started up; he was the first to arrive there in his canoe, the Pukeatea-wai-nui, for he had been left behind by the Arawa, and his wife Whakaoti-rangi had been carried off by Tama-te-kapua. After the Arawa had left he sailed in his own canoe for these islands, landed at Maketu, and his canoe reached land the first. He started up, cast his line into the sea with the hooks attached to it, and they got fast in one of the beams of the Arawa, and it was pulled ashore by him whilst the crew were asleep; the hundred and forty men who accompanied him stood upon the beach with skids all ready laid, and the Arawa was dragged upon the shore in the night and left there. Ruaeo seated himself under the side of the Arawa and played upon his flute; the music woke his wife, who said, 'Dear me, that's Rua'!', and they passed the night together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Rua' said, 'O mother of my children, go back now to your new husband, and presently I'll play upon the flute and putorino, so that both you and Tama-te-kapua may hear. Then do you say to Tama-te-kapua, O! I had a dream in the night that I heard Rua playing a tune upon his flute' - and that will make him so jealous that he will give you a blow, and then you can run away from him as if you were in a rage and hurt, and come to me.' She did everything exactly as Rua' had told her; Tama' began to beat her and she ran away from him. Early in the morning Rua' performed incantations by which he kept all the people in the canoe in a profound sleep, and whilst they slept the sun rose and mounted high in the heavens. In the forenoon Rua' gave the canoe a heavy blow with his club; they all started up - it was almost noon, and when they looked down over the edge of their canoe, there were the hundred and forty men of Rua' sitting under them, all beautifully dressed with feathers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Rua' shouted out as he stood, 'Come here, Tama-te-kapua; let us two fight the battle, you and I alone. If you are stronger than I am, well and good; if I am stronger than you are, I'll dash you to the earth.' Up sprang the hero Tama-te-kapua with a carved two-handed sword decked with red feathers; Rua' held a similar weapon. Tama' first struck a fierce blow; Rua' parried it, threw away his sword, seized both Tama's arms and dashed him to the earth. Tama' half rose and was again dashed down; once more he almost rose and was thrown again; still he fiercely struggled to rise. For the fourth time he almost rose up; then Rua', overcome with rage, took a heap of vermin he had prepared to cover Tama' with insult and shame, and rubbed them on Tama-te-kapua's head and ear, and they adhered so fast that Tama' tried in vain to get them out. Rua' said, 'There, I've beaten you; now keep the woman, as a payment for the insults I've heaped upon you and for having been beaten by me'; but Tama', driven almost mad with the pain and itching, could do nothing but stand scratching his head, whilst Rua' departed with his hundred and forty men to seek some other dwelling-place. These men were giants - Tama-te-kapua was nine feet high, Rua' was eleven feet high; there have been no men since that time so tall as those heroes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
